title: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Clues: 4.1.1-c27 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.1.1-c31 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.1.1-c36 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.1.1-c32 first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Atomic number
items.clue: The number of protons in an atom of an element.

items.label: Mass number
items.clue: The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom.

items.label: Electronic structure
items.clue: The arrangement written as numbers such as 2,8,1 for sodium.

items.label: Isotopes
items.clue: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

questions.stem: Which statement describes what an atom is?

options.text: The smallest part of an element that can exist
The smallest particle that can ever exist
The smallest part of any compound that exists
A particle made of two or more atoms joined

questions.explanation: This is the specification's definition of an atom.

questions.stem: Which option gives the chemical symbols correctly?

options.text: So is sodium and Ox is oxygen
Na is sodium and O is oxygen
N is sodium and O is oxygen
Na is sodium, O2 is oxygen

questions.explanation: Na represents an atom of sodium and O an atom of oxygen.

questions.stem: About how many different elements are there, and where are they shown?

options.text: About 100 elements and compounds, shown in the table
About 20 elements only, all shown in the periodic table
About 100 elements, all shown in the periodic table
Many thousands of elements, most not in the table

questions.explanation: Matches the specification: about 100 elements, shown in the periodic table.

questions.stem: Which statement about a compound is correct?

options.text: Its elements can be mixed together in any proportions at all
Its elements keep all the properties they had before mixing
Its elements can be separated from it by simple filtration
Its elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions

questions.explanation: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.

questions.stem: What must happen in every chemical reaction?

options.text: A detectable energy change must be measured
One or more new substances must always be formed
A gas or a change of colour must be seen
Two elements must join to make a compound

questions.explanation: Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances.

questions.stem: How can a compound be separated into its elements?

options.text: Only by using a chemical reaction
By filtering it through filter paper
By evaporating the liquid away from it
By distilling the compound in a flask

questions.explanation: Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.

questions.stem: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride and hydrogen. Which is the correct word equation?

options.text: magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + water
Mg + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
magnesium + HCl → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

questions.explanation: Reactant names on the left, product names on the right, all written as words.

questions.stem: A compound has the formula MgO. What is its name?

options.text: Magnesium oxygen
Magnesium oxide
Magnesium dioxide
Magnesium monoxide

questions.explanation: The metal keeps its name and oxygen becomes oxide.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which symbol equation represents this reaction correctly?

options.text: Mg + O₂ → MgO
Mg + O₂ → MgO₂
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2Mg + 2O₂ → 2MgO

questions.explanation: Two Mg atoms and two O atoms on each side, with the products on the right.

questions.stem: (HT only) Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows what happens at the positive electrode?

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
Br⁻ + e⁻ → Br₂
Br⁻ + Br⁻ → Br₂ + e⁻
2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻

questions.explanation: Two bromide ions lose two electrons and form a bromine molecule.

questions.stem: (HT only) Silver nitrate solution reacts with sodium chloride solution: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq). Which is the correct ionic equation?

options.text: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
Ag⁺(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)
AgNO₃(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
Na⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq) → NaNO₃(aq)

questions.explanation: Only these ions change; Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions and are left out.
